---

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (circa 1780–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Period covered:** Primarily the Mississippi Territory phase (1798–1817) and the Alabama Territory (1817–1819), with colonial background from the Spanish period (1780–1813) in the Mobile area.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial capital at Washington, Mississippi Territory; Mobile was the dominant Gulf Coast settlement.
- **Parent jurisdictions over time:**
  - French colony (Mobile founded 1702; French to 1763)
  - British West Florida (1763–1780)
  - Spanish Mobile District (1780–1813)
  - Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) — the Alabama portion was in the eastern half
  - Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
  - State of Alabama (1819–present)
- **Population:** Sparse and scattered at 1800; the region saw rapid in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after the Creek War of 1813–1814. The 1810 federal census was the first to enumerate the area.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, cotton cultivation beginning to take hold, river trade, and coastal commerce at Mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** American settlers (principally of Scots-Irish, English, and German ancestry) arriving from the Upper South; French Creole and Spanish Creole communities centered on Mobile; Creek and Cherokee nations throughout much of the interior.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist and Methodist circuit riders were the primary denominations serving frontier settlers; Catholic parishes in Mobile predating American control.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish cession of Mobile (1813), Creek War (1813–1814), land cession treaties with the Creek and Cherokee, rapid territorial land surveys and patent filings after 1814.

## Boundary changes

This is the most critical complexity for pre-statehood Alabama research. The jurisdictional history runs as three overlapping layers:

1. **Before 1798 (eastern Alabama interior):** No organized American civil authority existed. Records were created by Creek and Cherokee tribal governments, British colonial courts (pre-1780), or not at all.
2. **Spanish Mobile District (1780–1813):** The Mobile coastal zone was administered by Spain. Spanish colonial records were created independently of any American territorial system and are held in separate repositories (see below).
3. **Mississippi Territory (1798–1817):** The full present-day Alabama area was the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory. Courts, land offices, and tax lists were organized at the territorial and county level. County formation began with Washington County (1800) and Madison County (1809) as the first counties carved from the Alabama portion of the territory.
4. **Alabama Territory (1817–1819):** The eastern half of the Mississippi Territory was reorganized as a separate territory, inheriting the existing county structure.

A record created around 1800 in the Alabama interior may be filed under Mississippi Territory / Washington County. The same geographic location falls under Alabama statehood records from 1819 onward. Always search under the predecessor jurisdiction first. The FamilySearch wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records confirms territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 were taken and are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Alabama did not have statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1908 (at the state level). Marriage registration at the county level began when individual counties were formed — the earliest Alabama county marriages on FamilySearch begin in 1809 (Washington County). There was no territorial-era civil birth or death registration.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection ID 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images, 1,224,690 persons). The earliest records in this collection correspond to the first organized counties in the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, indexed); county probate courts hold originals.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration for the 1800 period at any level. Marriage bonds and licenses are the only civil vital records available for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); family Bible entries; estate inventories that name heirs and spouses.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, from French colonial period); Baptist and Methodist (frontier circuits, interior settlements from roughly 1808 onward).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Catholic registers in Mobile are the most comprehensive for the pre-1813 period.
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic records for the Mobile area: Diocese of Mobile archives; originals and microfilm also at Mobile Municipal Archives and copied at the Library of Congress (Spanish-era registers).
  - Baptist and Methodist circuit records: denomination archives; some on FamilySearch microfilm.
  - FamilySearch holds **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection ID 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images).
- **Language:** Catholic registers from the Spanish period are in Spanish and Latin. French colonial registers are in French.

### Census records

- **Territorial censuses (Mississippi Territory):** Enumerations of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 covered the Alabama portion. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery. Per the FamilySearch wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records, they are the primary census-type source for the 1800 period.
- **Federal census — 1810:** The first federal census to enumerate the Alabama area was 1810, while it was still the Mississippi Territory. Returns for the Alabama counties are included in the published Mississippi Territory census.
- **Federal census — 1820:** The first census taken after statehood (1819); Alabama appears as its own state entry.
- **Compiled index:** FamilySearch holds **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection ID 2016756; 287,634 records; images not digitized — index only).
- **Access:** The compiled index is name-searchable; original territorial census images at ADAH are physical.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, and court minutes from territorial county courts.
- **Date range:** Washington County (formed 1800) is the earliest Alabama-area county with organized court records. FamilySearch holds **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection ID 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images).
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch has 2 digitized volumes matching the 1780–1820 window:
  - Volume 004512889 — 214 images, covering Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819. **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
  - Volume 004512890 — 96 images, covering Washington County, Alabama deed and probate records, 1803–1820. **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** County probate courts hold originals; ADAH holds many early territorial records.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state (public land survey system — township, range, and section). The General Land Office (GLO) administered land patents after the land cession treaties with the Creek and Cherokee nations, principally after 1814.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal GLO issued patents; these are searchable and viewable free at the Bureau of Land Management GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). The earliest Alabama land patents date from approximately 1817 onward for most of the interior.
- **Spanish and British grants (Mobile area):** Pre-American land titles in the Mobile coastal zone were granted under Spanish and British authority. These require separate research in Spanish archives (see Colonial records, below) and in territorial confirmation proceedings, which were recorded in the Mississippi Territory superior court.
- **Tax records as substitutes:** Territorial tax lists from 1809 onward are the closest substitute to a census for years between enumerations.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (patents, online free); ADAH (territorial era); county probate courts (deeds).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast theater, including the defense and capture of Mobile).
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls for the Mississippi Territory; service records and pension files at NARA (pension files are particularly rich for this period — veterans who survived into the 1820s–1840s filed depositions describing early settlement, marriages, and children).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and Southeast Regional facility in Morrow, Georgia); Fold3 online (subscription); ADAH holds some state adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries and family burial grounds were the norm for the frontier period; no large public cemeteries existed in the Alabama interior before statehood.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover some Alabama cemeteries; coverage for pre-1820 graves is sparse and dependent on volunteer transcription.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely exist for the period. The most reliable sources are tombstone surveys done by genealogical societies (held at ADAH and local libraries).

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** No newspaper is confirmed by tool results to have operated in the Alabama interior before statehood; the Mobile area had limited colonial-era print culture. Newspapers become relevant from the 1820s onward.
- **Access:** The Alabama Department of Archives and History holds the earliest Alabama newspaper runs on microfilm. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america) cover later periods.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the primary Gulf Coast port of entry for the region.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA cover post-1820 arrivals most completely. Naturalization records before 1906 could be filed in any court of record — the territorial superior court and county courts are the places to check for the 1800 period.
- **Colonial period:** Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District named heads of household and sometimes family members; these documents function as both census and immigration records for the Spanish period (1780–1813). Per the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), originals are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville; copies are at the Library of Congress.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists, when they exist, record every person aboard including children traveling with parents — always examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial property and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Tax lists for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory begin approximately 1809.
- **Where held:** ADAH; some on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the missing pre-1810 census for most of the Alabama interior.

### Colonial records (Spanish and French — Mobile area only)

This record class is unique to the pre-1813 Mobile coastal zone and does not apply to most of the Alabama interior.

- **French colonial records (1702–1763):** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Spanish colonial records (1780–1813):** Per the FamilySearch wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records — originals at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress. Types include census returns, church registers, and land grants.
- **Language:** French and Spanish. Researchers must be able to read the original language or commission a translation.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records 1809–1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810–1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records 1803–1950 (1986396); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (territorial court/land and Washington Co. deed/probate, 1803–1820) | Free |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Alabama federal land patents, principally post-1817 | Free |
| Fold3 | NARA military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Federal census (1810, 1820); compiled indexes | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions (sparse pre-1820) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes total for the 1780–1820 window — this is the complete result set (no further pages). The `collections_search` returned 4 indexed collections; all are listed above.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial tax lists; county records transferred from courthouse; state records post-1819 | In-person; some materials via written request; online catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| National Archives — Southeast Region, Morrow, Georgia | Federal court records; some territorial records | In-person; written request |
| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Military service records; pension files; War of 1812 records; GLO correspondence | In-person; written request; many pension files on Fold3 |
| Washington County Probate Court, Chatom, Alabama | Original deed books and probate files from 1800 (earliest Alabama county) | In-person; written request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial microfilm; local records | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized through Portal de Archivos Espanoles (pares.mcu.es) |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Copies of French and Spanish colonial records for the Mobile area | In-person; some online |
| Diocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers, Mobile, from colonial period | Written inquiry |

## Records NOT online

The following are known to exist but are not available in any current online name-indexed database:

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (ADAH, physical only)
- Washington County deed and probate records 1803–1820 (digitized on FamilySearch as browse-only images — volume 004512890 — but 0% indexed; must be browsed page by page)
- Alabama territorial court and land records 1808–1819 (digitized on FamilySearch as browse-only images — volume 004512889 — but 0% indexed; must be browsed page by page)
- French colonial records (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias; partial copies at Library of Congress; some accessible via pares.mcu.es)
- Baptist and Methodist circuit records not yet microfilmed or digitized

## Known record losses

- No specific courthouse fire losses are confirmed by tool results for Washington County or the territorial period. Alabama has generally had fewer catastrophic courthouse fires than some Deep South states, but researchers should verify the specific county's loss history at ADAH before concluding a record never existed.
- Spanish colonial records were partially dispersed at the transfer of Mobile to American control in 1813; not all copies made it to American repositories.

## Research tips

- **Always begin with the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.** The first organized counties in the Alabama area — Washington (1800) and Baldwin (1809) — were Mississippi Territory counties. Land records, court records, and tax lists for any event before 1817 will be filed under "Mississippi Territory" or a specific county thereof, not under "Alabama." Searching only Alabama will miss the earliest available records. (Source: FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **The 1810 federal census is the earliest federal enumeration for this area.** It was taken while the region was still the Mississippi Territory; look in the Mississippi Territory returns for Alabama-area counties, not in a separate Alabama entry.
- **Pension files are among the richest sources for this period.** A settler who served in the Creek War or War of 1812 and survived to the 1820s–1850s would have filed a pension application that often includes a deposition describing where he lived, whom he married, when, and naming children. These can substitute for missing vital records. Access via NARA or Fold3.
- **For the Mobile area specifically, research requires a multi-archive, multi-language approach.** French records (French), Spanish records (Spanish and Latin), and American territorial records (English) all cover overlapping time periods and populations in the Mobile coastal zone. A settler in Mobile around 1800 lived under Spanish rule; civil and church records for that event are in Spanish repositories.
- **Federal land patents were not issued until after treaty-era surveys (principally 1817 onward) for most of the interior.** A settler farming land in 1800 may appear in territorial tax lists or court records long before a patent appears at the BLM GLO.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** The Alabama area bordered the Spanish Floridas to the south and east, the Georgia frontier to the east, and the Tennessee frontier to the north. A family near these borders likely generated records on multiple sides. Georgia state land lotteries (1805–1832) and Georgia court records document families who later moved into the Alabama territory.
- **The FamilySearch wiki article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy is the primary reference guide** for Alabama research. The topical wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs all resolved to a generic page rather than Alabama-specific content during this survey — a coverage gap in the wiki for those sub-topics as of this survey date (October 2026). Consult the main Alabama Genealogy article and ADAH directly for authoritative detail.

---

At that date the area was formally the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory, and the very first counties (Washington County, formed 1800) had only just been organized, so the earliest surviving records are sparse. For anyone in the Mobile coastal zone, research must also extend to Spanish and French colonial archives — the Archivo General de Indias in Seville and the Library of Congress hold the most important colonial records. Two digitized volumes of early Alabama records are on FamilySearch but are browse-only with no name index, meaning they must be paged through image by image. ## Arkansas Region Under Spanish Control (c. 1763–1800)

This survey covers the Arkansas region during the Spanish colonial period (1763–1800), when the entire district consisted of a single small settlement — **Arkansas Post** — administered as part of **Spanish Louisiana** from New Orleans.

The European population was tiny, and the kinds of records a researcher typically turns to (county courthouses, statewide vital registration, federal census) simply did not exist yet. What survives is a thin but real record base:

- **One digitized volume of Catholic sacramental registers** on FamilySearch that must be browsed image by image in Spanish.
- **A larger body of padrones (censuses), land concessions, military rosters, and commandant correspondence** that exists only in physical or microfilm form — split primarily between:
  - **Arkansas History Commission** in Little Rock, Arkansas (ark-ives.com for finding aids)
  - **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain

### Key Reorientation

The critical shift for this period is to **work through New Orleans, not through Arkansas**: all administrative records flowed to the colonial capital, and many Arkansas Post individuals appear nowhere in Arkansas-specific holdings but turn up in the **Louisiana colonial collections** and in Seville. 

### Accessible Starting Points

- **PARES online portal** (pares.mcu.es) — Spain's Ministry of Culture provides free access to digitized finding aids and some documents from the Archivo General de Indias. Search for "Arkanzas" or the Arkansas Post commandant's name.
- **Arkansas History Commission** (ark-ives.com) — holds the most accessible portion of the surviving Arkansas-specific record base for this period.
- **FamilySearch Catholic registers** — must be browsed image by image; records are in Spanish.

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Start at the Arkansas History Commission and search their finding aids for Arkansas Post materials.
2. Search the PARES portal for documents referencing "Arkanzas" or the Arkansas Post commandant.
3. Extend the search to Louisiana colonial collections in New Orleans for individuals who may not appear in Arkansas-specific holdings.

These two sources together cover the most accessible portion of the surviving record base for this period.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region under Spanish Colonial Administration (Pre-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas came under Spanish authority by the Treaty of Paris in 1763, transferred from French Louisiana. Spain administered it as Spanish Louisiana until secretly ceding it back to France in 1800; France sold it to the United States in 1803 (Louisiana Purchase). Arkansas became a state in 1836.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Puesto de los Arkanzas), established 1686, was the sole significant European settlement and the seat of all civil and military administration.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Spanish Louisiana (colonial), superior capital at New Orleans; imperial bureaucracy reported to the Capitanía General of Cuba and to Madrid.
- **Population during period:** Extremely small European settler population (dozens to a few hundred); documented in Spanish padrones (census lists).
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur and deerskin trade, Mississippi/Arkansas River commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, small Spanish military garrison, French-Canadian fur traders, free persons of color, enslaved Africans, and multiple Native American nations (Quapaw, Osage, Caddo). Anglo-American settlers arrived in the 1790s under Spanish land grants.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively; served by French Capuchin and Recollect missionaries under the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas (New Orleans/Havana).
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris 1763 (French-to-Spanish); Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800 (Spanish-to-French); Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: French Louisiana — records in French colonial archives.
- 1763–1800: Spanish Louisiana — records in Spanish, held in New Orleans, Havana, and Seville.
- 1800–1803: Retroceded to France briefly.
- Post-1803: U.S. territorial governance; American record series begins.
- No internal county divisions existed during the Spanish period — all records are at the post/district level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in Spanish colonial Arkansas. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Vital Records did not return specific content for this survey.
- **What exists:** No government-mandated civil vital records. Catholic sacramental registers are the functional equivalent.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below) are the primary vital-event documentation.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only.
- **Record types:** Baptismal, marriage, burial, and confirmation registers.
- **What digitized:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763–1800, image group 008814402, 64 images. Browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). In Spanish/Latin.
- **Where also held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (registers); Arkansas History Commission (transcribed form).
- **Language:** Spanish and ecclesiastical Latin; earlier French-era registers in French.

### Census records (padrones)
- **Spanish padrones:** Household censuses listing family members, ages, occupations, racial designations.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias, Seville; microfilm at Library of Congress.
- **Digitization:** Not in FamilySearch indexed collections. Physical/microfilm only.
- **Federal census:** First federal coverage of Arkansas was 1810 (territorial). The FamilySearch Arkansas Compiled Census collection (2085124) begins in 1819 and does not cover the Spanish period.

### Land records
- **System:** Spanish concession (land grant) system issued by the governor at New Orleans.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish governor of Louisiana at New Orleans; local administration by the Arkansas Post commandant.
- **Types:** Land concessions, land petitions, associated administrative correspondence.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission; post-1803 U.S. adjudications at NARA and BLM GLO website.
- **Digitization:** Spanish-era concessions not in FamilySearch collections. Physical/microfilm only for the colonial series.

### Military records
- **Relevant context:** Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison throughout this period.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, service records (hojas de servicio), payrolls, commandant correspondence.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Arkansas History Commission (microfilm/transcripts).
- **Digitization:** Not represented in FamilySearch Arkansas collections. Physical/microfilm only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Commandant's court records: civil disputes, estate inventories, contracts, manumissions (notarial acts).
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; New Orleans Notarial Archives; Louisiana State Archives; Arkansas History Commission.
- **Digitization:** Not in FamilySearch Arkansas collections. Physical/microfilm only.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Movement tracked through commandant correspondence and padrones rather than formal immigration records. Anglo-American settlers in the 1790s appear in land concession files.
- **Record types:** Commandant correspondence naming arrivals; land concession petitions identifying settlers' origins; loyalty oaths.
- **Where held:** Same as land records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemetery at Arkansas Post.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave covers the modern site but has no systematic coverage of pre-1800 interments.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries appear in the sacramental registers (FamilySearch image group 008814402). Diocese of Little Rock holds additional register materials.

### Newspaper records
- No newspaper publication existed in the Arkansas district during the Spanish period.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts:** Commandant-as-notary records (contracts, sales, manumissions, inventories) in colonial archive collections named above.
- **Commandant correspondence:** Substantial body of documentation naming settlers; held at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century local histories sometimes transcribe colonial-era lists and padrones; at the Arkansas History Commission library.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place and period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, image group 008814402, 64 images — browse-only, Spanish/Latin | Free |
| PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) | Selected digitized documents from the Archivo General de Indias, including some Louisiana/Arkansas colonial records | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Post-1803 adjudications of Spanish-era land claims — indirect route to Spanish-period grantees | Free |
| NARA Online / Fold3 / Ancestry | Spanish land claim adjudication records and early territorial records | Subscription (Fold3, Ancestry) or free at NARA |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial padrones, land concessions, commandant correspondence (originals/microfilm), transcribed church registers | In-person; finding aids at ark-ives.com |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, AR | Sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Contact archives; appointment required |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Primary archive for Spanish colonial Louisiana: land concessions, military records, padrones, administrative correspondence | In-person or PARES online portal |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected Archivo General de Indias records | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives / Louisiana State Archives | Colonial Louisiana notarial records; some Arkansas Post-adjacent documents | In-person or written inquiry |
| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Post-1803 territorial records; Spanish land claim adjudications | In-person or NARA catalog online |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (censuses) for Arkansas Post
- Spanish land concession files and petitions
- Military muster rolls and service records of the Arkansas Post garrison
- Commandant correspondence and notarial acts
- Estate/probate inventories from the commandant's court
- Loyalty oaths and travel documents

## Known record losses
- Survival of Arkansas Post records is fragmentary. The settlement was small and subject to periodic flooding; some documents were lost to environmental damage.
- The bulk of the surviving administrative record was transmitted to Seville and was not retained locally after the Louisiana Purchase.
- No specific inventory of destroyed or lost record sets was returned by the tools used in this survey; substantial gaps should be assumed.

## Research tips
- Work through New Orleans, not through Arkansas: the administrative capital was New Orleans, and Arkansas Post records went there. Research in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Louisiana colonial collections will often surface Arkansas Post residents absent from Arkansas-specific collections. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- The PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) has digitized selected Archivo General de Indias documents; search 'Arkanzas' or 'Poste des Arkan' for colonial-era documents.
- Use Spanish land claim adjudications filed post-1803 (NARA/BLM GLO) as a back-door into Spanish-period land grant data.
- Padrones are the primary population-finding tool and are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias.
- Records are in Spanish, Latin, and French — 18th-century paleography expertise or a professional translator is required.
- Enslaved persons appear in Catholic baptismal registers and notarial estate inventories.
- Neighboring Spanish posts (Natchez, St. Louis, Natchitoches) also generated records naming Arkansas Post-area individuals.

| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected Archivo General de Indias records | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives / Louisiana State Archives | Colonial Louisiana notarial records; some Arkansas Post-adjacent documents | In-person or written inquiry |
| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Post-1803 territorial records; Spanish land claim adjudications | In-person or NARA catalog online |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (censuses) for Arkansas Post
- Spanish land concession files and petitions
- Military muster rolls and service records of the Arkansas Post garrison
- Commandant correspondence and notarial acts
- Estate/probate inventories from the commandant's court
- Loyalty oaths and travel documents

## Known record losses
- Survival of Arkansas Post records is fragmentary. The settlement was small and subject to periodic flooding; some documents were lost to environmental damage.
- The bulk of the surviving administrative record was transmitted to Seville and was not retained locally after the Louisiana Purchase.
- No specific inventory of destroyed or lost record sets was returned by the tools used in this survey; substantial gaps should be assumed.

## Research tips
- Work through New Orleans, not through Arkansas: the administrative capital was New Orleans, and Arkansas Post records went there. Research in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Louisiana colonial collections will often surface Arkansas Post residents absent from Arkansas-specific collections. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- The PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) has digitized selected Archivo General de Indias documents; search 'Arkanzas' or 'Poste des Arkan' for colonial-era documents.
- Use Spanish land claim adjudications filed post-1803 (NARA/BLM GLO) as a back-door into Spanish-period land grant data.
- Padrones are the primary population-finding tool and are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias.
- Records are in Spanish, Latin, and French — 18th-century paleography expertise or a professional translator is required.
- Enslaved persons appear in Catholic baptismal registers and notarial estate inventories.
- Neighboring Spanish posts (Natchez, St. Louis, Natchitoches) also generated records naming Arkansas Post-area individuals.

Here is the locality guide returned by the specialist agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Period, c. 1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview

At 1790, Ohio did not exist as a state — it was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, administered from Marietta and later Cincinnati. Ohio achieved statehood on **1 March 1803**. The first federal census in 1790 counted only ~3,000 non-Native American settlers in the territory.

Settlers came predominantly from Virginia, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, and New England. Major religious denominations included Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, and German Reformed — though formal church infrastructure was sparse on the frontier.

---

## Boundary Changes

This is a period of rapid, overlapping county formations. The county of jurisdiction matters enormously because **all civil records were kept at the county level**:

- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River (and more). All records before any later formation fall here.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covering southwestern Ohio (Cincinnati area, Virginia Military District lands west of the Scioto River).
- **1795 onward:** Additional counties (Knox, etc.) carved out rapidly after the Treaty of Greenville opened more land.

**Critical rule:** Determine which county had jurisdiction over your ancestor's *specific location* at the *specific date* of the event before searching any record type. The same geographic area could shift county jurisdiction within just a few years.

---

## Land District Split — Three Separate Systems

Ohio land records are divided geographically among **three distinct survey systems**, each with records in a different repository:

| District | Location | Survey type | Records held at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds | Virginia State Library, Richmond |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Separate grid (Connecticut Land Co.) | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **Federal public domain lands** | Remainder | Rectangular (township-range) | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |

Searching only Ohio repositories when your ancestor was in the Virginia Military District means finding nothing — even though records exist.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No statewide civil registration existed in 1790** — births and deaths were simply never recorded civilly during the territorial period. This is not a record loss; the records were never created.
- **County marriages begin in 1789.** FamilySearch collection **"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (ID 1803785; 1.5M records): [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785)
- **Primary substitutes for births/deaths:** Church baptism and burial records (see below).

### Church Records
- Earliest indexed collection: **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (ID 2246917; 678K records): [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) — begins before statehood and is the earliest fully indexed Ohio collection.
- Caution: Church infrastructure was minimal on the frontier; records may be thin or absent for the earliest years.

### Census Records
- The **1790 federal census did not reliably enumerate the Northwest Territory.** Do not expect to find 1790 Ohio census entries.
- The **1800 federal census** is the first reliably available enumeration for Ohio — use it as the earliest practical federal census anchor.
- **Substitute for the missing 1790 enumeration:** Tax lists (see below).

### Land Records
- FamilySearch collection **"Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"** (ID 1542187; 235K records): [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) — begins in 1787, covering the territorial period.
- **Land records are often the single most important source for 1790-era Ohio ancestors** — a land entry places a person at a specific location on a specific date, often naming neighbors and witnesses.
- Virginia Military District warrants and Connecticut Reserve records require separate repository access (see table above).

### Probate and Court Records
- Territorial court records begin at **Washington County (1788)**.
- Early territorial court records are held at the **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus).
- Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes, partially indexed or browse-only.

### Tax Records
- FamilySearch collection **"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (ID 1987542; 346K records) starts in 1800 — not 1790.
- Washington County tax records 1799–1803 exist in digitized form (12% name-indexed; rest browse-only).
- **Tax lists are the primary substitute for the absent 1790 territorial census.**

### Military Records
- Many Ohio settlers were **Revolutionary War veterans** receiving bounty land in the Virginia Military District.
- Revolutionary War service records and pension files: NARA / [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)
- Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) territorial militia records also at NARA.

### Newspapers
- The first Ohio territory newspaper (*Centinel of the North-Western Territory*, Cincinnati) began in **1793** — nothing before that date.
- Pre-1800 coverage on Newspapers.com is minimal.

### Other Records
- **Territorial court minutes** name ordinary residents appearing in no other record type (road assignments, poor relief, appointments). At the Ohio History Connection.
- **Surveyor plats and field notes** may name an occupant or claimant who doesn't yet appear in a deed. At BLM and Ohio History Connection.
- **Published county histories** (19th century) often contain pioneer family sketches and transcriptions of early records since lost. Search [HathiTrust](https://hathitrust.org) and [Internet Archive](https://archive.org) by county name.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Marriages 1789+, Church 1787+, Land 1787+, Tax 1800+ | Free |
| Ancestry | 1800 federal census; Revolutionary War records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service files, pension records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse for 1790 period) | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial court records, land records, state archives |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrants |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Reserve land records |
| Washington Co. / Hamilton Co. courthouses | Deed books, probate, court minutes from formation |
| NARA (DC/regional) | Federal military, pension, naturalization records |

---

## Known Gaps and Record Losses

- **No civil birth or death registration in 1790** — not a loss, never created.
- **1790 federal census unreliable** for the Northwest Territory — absence is normal.
- **Records 1785–1788** (before Washington County's formation) are the most likely to be absent — territorial record-keeping was inconsistent and survival rates are low.
- No specific courthouse-fire losses are confirmed for early territorial Ohio counties, but verify with individual county historical societies.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Determine the county first.** No county = no records. Establish which county held jurisdiction at the specific location and year before searching anything.
2. **Know your land district.** Virginia Military District → Virginia State Library. Connecticut Reserve → WRHS Cleveland. Federal lands → BLM GLO. Wrong repository = no results even when records exist.
3. **Trace back to the origin state.** Most 1790 Ohio settlers came from Virginia, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, or Kentucky, where the richer documentary record (birth, marriage, church) exists. Use Ohio land and tax records to confirm presence, then work backward.
4. **Church records are the earliest substitute** for missing vital registration. Search "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" before concluding no records exist.
5. **Use the 1800 census as your first reliable federal enumeration** — the 1790 territorial count is too incomplete to rely on.
6. **Published county histories** may be the only surviving source for some territorial-era families. Search HathiTrust and Internet Archive by county name.

---

The logical next step is to narrow to the specific county and land district where your ancestor was located, then target that county's records alongside the appropriate land-grant repository.

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Period, c. 1785-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Governing jurisdiction at 1790:** Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio as a state did not exist — the future state of Ohio was administered as part of the Northwest Territory until statehood on 1 March 1803.
- **Territorial capital:** Marietta (1788), later Cincinnati
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States federal government (Congress held authority over the Northwest Territory)
- **Population during period:** Population data for this specific standardPlace and period was not returned by the population tool, indicating no indexed figures in that system for pre-statehood Ohio. The first federal census in 1790 counted approximately 3,000 non-Native American settlers in the territory; by 1800 that had grown substantially, concentrated around Marietta, Cincinnati, and the early river settlements.
- **Economy:** Frontier agriculture, land speculation, fur trade, Ohio River commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American migrants from Virginia, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, and New England; smaller numbers of German-speaking settlers
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, and German Reformed congregations were among the earliest; formal church infrastructure was sparse before the early 1800s
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787), founding of Marietta (1788), Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), Treaty of Greenville (1795, opening more land to settlement), Ohio statehood (1803)

---

## Boundary changes

This period involves a series of rapid, overlapping geographic splits — not a single clean temporal transition. Which county held jurisdiction over any given event depends on exactly where within the territory the event occurred and in which year.

**Sequence of county formations from the Northwest Territory:**

- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River and much more. All records before any later county formation are under Washington County.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covering southwestern Ohio (the Cincinnati area and the Virginia Military District lands west of the Scioto River). Any event in that region after 1790 is under Hamilton County, not Washington County.
- **1795 onward:** Additional counties were carved out rapidly as settlement expanded and the Treaty of Greenville opened new land. Knox County and others followed.

**Critical rule for researchers:** There were no state-level records in 1790 — everything filed was at the territorial county level. Determine which county had jurisdiction over the specific location at the specific date of the event, then search that county's records. The county of jurisdiction can change within just a few years for the same geographic location. The Ohio History Connection in Columbus (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki search results at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory) holds early court and land records.

**Land grant systems — a geographic split within the territory:** The territory was divided among distinct survey systems whose records are held in entirely different repositories:

- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): Used metes-and-bounds. Land warrants for this district are at the Virginia State Library in Richmond, not Ohio repositories. Confirmed by wiki_search results.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Surveyed on a separate grid by Connecticut. Records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland. Confirmed by wiki_search results.
- **United States Military District** and other federal lands: Rectangular survey (township-range). Patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website.

Which system applies depends on where in Ohio your ancestor settled — these are geographic splits, not temporal ones. You cannot assume one repository holds all land records.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Ohio did not have statewide civil registration of births and deaths in 1790, and did not require it during the territorial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records resolved only to a generic fallback page and did not return Ohio-specific registration dates. Based on the wiki_search and Wikipedia results, no statewide civil vital registration system existed for Ohio in 1790. The FamilySearch-indexed collection **"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013"** (Collection ID 1803785; 1,523,678 records; ~761,839 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) begins in 1789 — consistent with early county-level marriage recording starting with Washington County's formation. This is the earliest civil record type confirmed available for the territorial period.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records from 1789. Births and deaths were not formally registered during the territorial period — no civil registration of those events is confirmed by the tools for this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouse records; FamilySearch has indexed and imaged the county marriage collection noted above.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration existed in Ohio in 1790. This is not a record loss — the records were simply never created.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial records are the primary substitute. See Church Records below.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, and German Reformed congregations are documented in the Ohio area by 1790, though formal church structures were minimal on the frontier.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (substitute for births), marriages, burials (substitute for deaths), membership rolls
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has indexed collection **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950"** (Collection ID 2246917; 678,234 records; ~339,117 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). This collection begins in 1787 and is the earliest Ohio-specific digitized collection confirmed by the tools. Denominational archives (e.g., Methodist conference archives, Presbyterian synod records) also hold materials.
- **Language:** English for most Protestant denominations in this Anglo-American settlement zone
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection above)
- **Important note:** Church infrastructure on the Ohio frontier in 1790 was sparse. Not all settlers were affiliated with a formal congregation, and records may be thin or absent for the earliest years.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory in the same way it enumerated the original states — territorial enumeration was incomplete and inconsistent. The 1800 federal census is the first reliably available enumeration for the Ohio territory. Researchers should not expect to find ancestors in a 1790 Ohio census.
- **Territorial enumerations:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Census resolved only to generic fallback content and did not confirm any territorial-era census distinct from the federal enumeration.
- **Access:** The 1800 federal census is indexed and searchable via Ancestry and FamilySearch for Ohio.
- **Substitute:** Tax lists (see Tax Records below) are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 enumeration.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, court minutes, and territorial court proceedings
- **Jurisdiction:** Filed at the county level. Before county formation (pre-1788), the territorial court based at Marietta had jurisdiction. After 1788, Washington County Court; after 1790, Hamilton County Court for the southwestern portion.
- **Date range:** Washington County territorial court records begin 1788.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (formerly Ohio Historical Society) in Columbus holds many early court and land records — confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki search results. County probate courts (successor institutions) hold subsequent records.
- **Access level:** Volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for this place and period. Neither is fully indexed. Browse-only for those volumes.

### Land records

- **Survey systems:** Three distinct systems apply — see Boundary Changes above. The system that applies depends on where in Ohio your ancestor settled.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:**
  - Virginia Military District: Virginia state government granted the warrants; records at Virginia State Library (Richmond)
  - Connecticut Western Reserve: Connecticut Land Company; records at Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland)
  - Federal public domain lands: U.S. General Land Office; patents searchable at BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, warrants, deeds, territorial land entries
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has indexed collection **"Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840"** (Collection ID 1542187; 234,567 records; ~117,283 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187), beginning in 1787 and thus covering the territorial period.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection above). Virginia Military District warrants and Connecticut Reserve records require separate physical or archival repository access.
- **Critical note:** Land records are often the single most important source for 1790-era Ohio ancestors. A land entry places a person at a specific location at a specific date and may name neighbors or legal witnesses.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (veterans arriving as settlers), Northwest Indian War (1785-1795 — engagements in Ohio territory)
- **Record types:**
  - Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA, Washington DC; also searchable on Fold3.com and Ancestry.com)
  - Bounty land warrants — many Ohio settlers received land in the Virginia Military District as Revolutionary War bounty land; the warrant is the key document
  - Northwest Indian War service records (territorial militia records at NARA)
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized many Revolutionary War pension and service files
- **Access level:** Federal military records at NARA — physical access or online via Fold3 (subscription). BLM GLO for bounty land warrant patents.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Frontier-era Ohio cemeteries are scattered and often unmarked or on private land. Formal public cemeteries were uncommon in 1790.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online source — transcriptions and photos contributed by volunteers; coverage of late-18th-century Ohio graves is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at local historical societies or county genealogical societies.
- **Realistic expectation:** Do not expect to find documented burials for 1790 Ohio ancestors in online databases. Cemetery visits or correspondence with local Ohio county genealogical societies is the most productive path.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in Ohio territory was the *Centinel of the North-Western Territory*, published in Cincinnati beginning 1793. Before 1793, no local newspaper existed in the Ohio territory.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some digitized Ohio historical papers, but coverage of pre-1800 Ohio papers is minimal.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, estate and legal notices, and pioneer community news; most useful for the 1800s rather than the 1790 period.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant routes:** Ohio Territory settlers arrived overland via the Forbes Road and Wilderness Road from Virginia/Kentucky, or by flatboat down the Ohio River, or by the Genesee Road from New York and New England.
- **Record types:** There were no formal immigration records for internal migrants moving from one U.S. state into the territory. If the ancestor emigrated from Europe, the relevant passenger list would be at an East Coast port of entry — not an Ohio record.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable to U.S.-born settlers. Foreign-born settlers could file declarations of intention in any court of record; territorial and county courts would have been the venue.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record arrivals at ports, not internal migration. Ohio-bound settlers are captured in origin-state records (Virginia, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, New York), not in Ohio arrival records.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial property and poll tax records; county tax duplicate lists
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has indexed collection **"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850"** (Collection ID 1987542; 345,890 records; ~172,945 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542). This collection starts in 1800, not 1790. For 1790-1799 tax records, the two digitized volumes returned by `volume_search` are relevant:
  - Image group 005112240: Washington County tax records, 1799-1803; 73 images; 12% name-indexed; not full-text searchable — **partially indexed, rest browse-only**
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the absent 1790 territorial census. A person on the tax list is confirmed present in the county in that year.
- **Where held:** County auditor / treasurer records at county courthouses; Ohio History Connection for early territorial records

### Other record types

- **Territorial court minutes:** The territorial courts recorded wide-ranging business — road assignments, poor relief, local appointments, and civil/criminal proceedings. These minutes name ordinary residents who appear in no other record type. Early territorial court records are at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Surveyor plats and field notes:** The original survey field notes for Ohio lands are at the Bureau of Land Management and at the Ohio History Connection. A surveyor's plat may name an occupant or claimant who does not yet appear in a deed.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published histories of Ohio counties frequently contain pioneer family sketches and transcriptions of early records since lost. Many are digitized at HathiTrust (hathitrust.org) and the Internet Archive (archive.org).
- **DNA evidence:** Given the extreme sparseness of 1790 documentary records, autosomal and Y-DNA testing can connect descendants to documented colonial Virginia, Pennsylvania, or New England lines — particularly valuable for tracing back through the Virginia Military District settlers.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections confirmed for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages 1789-2013 (ID 1803785; 1.5M records); Ohio, Church Records 1787-1950 (ID 2246917; 678K records); Ohio, Land Records 1787-1840 (ID 1542187; 235K records); Ohio, Tax Records 1800-1850 (ID 1987542; 346K records) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (including 1800 Ohio); Revolutionary War pensions and service records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (Revolutionary War pensions, service files) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (volunteer-contributed; sparse for 1790 period) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (minimal pre-1800 Ohio coverage) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military and naturalization records | Free to access in person; some digitized online |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes total for this place and period — that is the complete result set (`totalResults: 2`; no `nextPageToken`). | Virginia State Library and Archives, Richmond | Virginia Military District land warrants and grants for southwestern Ohio settlers | In-person or written request |

- Virginia Military District land warrants held at the Virginia State Library — not digitized in any confirmed online collection
- Connecticut Western Reserve land and settlement records at WRHS — not confirmed online
- Original territorial court minute books (Washington County, Hamilton County) — the Ohio History Connection holds these; online availability is not confirmed by the tools
- Surveyor field notes for original Ohio surveys — at BLM and Ohio History Connection; field notes are largely physical
- Local church records not yet microfilmed or contributed to FamilySearch

## Known record losses

- No courthouse-fire losses are specifically confirmed for territorial-era Ohio counties by the tools used in this survey. Washington County (Marietta) and Hamilton County (Cincinnati) both survived the territorial period, but the researcher should verify with individual county historical societies whether any early record series were lost.
- The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory comprehensively — the absence of your ancestor in 1790 census results is normal, not a gap to be resolved.
- Records for the period 1785-1788, before Washington County was organized, are the most likely to be absent: the territorial government was newly formed, record-keeping was inconsistent, and survival rates are low. Tax and land records are the most likely to survive from this stratum.

## Research tips

- **Determine the county first, always.** In 1790 Ohio, the county held all civil authority. Before searching any record type, establish which county had jurisdiction over your ancestor's location at the exact year. Washington County (formed 1788) covers eastern Ohio before any other county formed; Hamilton County (formed 1790) covers the southwest. A county that does not yet exist cannot hold a record. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Land records are the anchor.** Because no civil vital registration existed in 1790 and the census is unreliable, land grants and entries are typically the first confirmed documentary evidence for a territorial-era Ohio ancestor. Start with the BLM GLO for federal lands, and identify which land district your location falls in before choosing a repository.
- **Know your land district.** Virginia Military District records are in Richmond, Virginia — not Columbus, Ohio. Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland. If you search only Ohio repositories and your ancestor was in the wrong district, you will find nothing. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Trace the ancestor back through the origin state.** Most 1790 Ohio settlers arrived from Virginia, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, or Kentucky. The richer documentary record (birth, marriage, earlier land, church) almost certainly exists in the origin state rather than Ohio. Use Ohio land and tax records to confirm presence, then work backward to where the person came from.
- **Use the 1800 census as the earliest reliable federal enumeration.** The 1800 census is the first full federal count that reliably covers Ohio. If searching for someone "around 1790," the 1800 census is often the first useful documentary census anchor.
- **Church records predate everything else.** The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (ID 2246917) begins in 1787 and is the earliest fully indexed collection confirmed for this place. Search it before assuming no records exist.
- **Naming conventions:** The FamilySearch Wiki Naming Customs page for Ohio resolved to a generic fallback and did not return Ohio-specific guidance. The settler population was predominantly Anglo-American; patronymic naming was not common in this population. No jurisdiction-specific naming quirk is confirmed by tool results — consult origin-state naming patterns instead.
- **Published county histories.** Nineteenth-century Ohio county histories often contain the only surviving transcriptions of early territorial-era records. Search HathiTrust and the Internet Archive by county name.

---

## Records NOT available (coverage note)

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs all resolved to a generic fallback page during this survey. No Ohio-specific wiki content was returned from those pages. For deeper Ohio-specific research guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy and the Ohio History Connection's online research guides at ohiohistory.org.

---

No `research.json` was found at the workspace path for this session, so no `localities` entry will be persisted — this is a standalone guide.

---

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means working in the Northwest Territory, not yet the state of Ohio. Only two counties had been organized by that year — Washington County (formed 1788, covering most of eastern Ohio) and Hamilton County (formed 1790, covering the southwest around Cincinnati). Civil government was thin, there was no vital registration of births or deaths, and the 1790 federal census did not reliably cover the territory. The records that do survive from this period — and there are meaningful ones — include county marriage records beginning in 1789, church records beginning in 1787, land grants and patents filed under three different land district systems (each with its records in a different physical repository), and county tax lists. The most important practical warning is that Ohio land records are split across Virginia, Connecticut, and federal systems depending on exactly where in Ohio your ancestor settled, so choosing the wrong repository means finding nothing even when records exist. The Ohio History Connection in Columbus holds the earliest territorial court and land records.

The logical next step is to narrow to the specific county and land district where your ancestor was located, then build a research plan targeting that county's records alongside the relevant land-grant repository — whether that is the Virginia State Library, the Western Reserve Historical Society, or the BLM General Land Office.

Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Statehood:** California was admitted to the Union on **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in Coloma on January 24, 1848.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the dominant commercial and port hub.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before statehood, California was ceded from Mexico by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848), then under brief U.S. military governance.
- **Population:** The Gold Rush drew approximately 300,000 people to California.
- **Ethnic composition:** Extremely diverse — migrants from the eastern U.S., Latin America (Chile, Mexico), China, Australia, and Europe (Ireland, Germany, France, England). Indigenous Californian populations were present throughout.

---

## Boundary Changes

California entered the Union with its current general boundaries, but **county boundaries changed frequently** throughout the 1850s as the legislature carved new counties from existing ones. The original 27 counties of 1850 were subdivided repeatedly. A researcher must confirm which county encompassed a location **at the specific event date** — a location might have been in one county in 1850 and a different county by 1855.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **County births, 1850–1919** — ~789,456 indexed records with images on FamilySearch (collection 2017276) — *indexed + images, free*
- **County marriages, 1850–1952** — ~567,890 indexed records with images on FamilySearch (collection 1452832) — *indexed + images, free*
- **Death registration gap:** No indexed death collection for the 1850s appeared in results. The transient mining population was often not registered at all.
- **Alternatives:** Mortality schedules attached to the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses record deaths in the year preceding enumeration.

### Census Records

- **1850 federal census:** Partially destroyed — some county returns are missing.
